summary: Describes the Extensible Provisioning Protocol, an XML-based client-server protocol for managing objects stored in a shared central repository, such as domain names at a registry. It defines generic operations and an extension framework for mapping them to object types. It was replaced by RFC 4930.

eli5.summary: Domain registries need a common way for companies to ask them to add, change or delete names. EPP is that common language, written in a structured text format.

questions: how do registrars talk to registries
how do registries manage domain registrations
how does extensible provisioning protocol work
subtitle: A language for provisioning systems to manage objects in a shared registry.

tldr.problem: Domain registries and other provisioning systems need a standardized way to manage objects such as domain names, contacts, and hosts stored in a central repository.
tldr.mechanism: EPP defines an XML-based client-server protocol that uses a set of generic operations (create, delete, query, update, renew, transfer) and an extension framework to map those operations to specific object types.
tldr.outcome: Registries and other operators have a common language for provisioning operations. RFC 4930 supersedes this specification with protocol version 1.0 updates.

today: RFC 3730 was the original EPP specification. It was replaced by RFC 4930, which includes updates and clarifications to the protocol specification.

sections.title: What EPP Is
sections.content:
EPP (Extensible Provisioning Protocol) is an application layer protocol for provisioning and managing objects stored in a central repository. It was originally designed to handle domain name registration at Internet registries, but it is flexible enough to manage any type of object.

The protocol operates as a stateful client-server exchange over a secure transport. A client logs in, exchanges commands and responses with the server, and then logs out. All commands are atomic—they either succeed completely or fail completely, with no partial results. Commands can be designed to be idempotent, so that repeating the same command produces the same outcome as running it once.
sections.eli5: EPP is like an online form for managing things. You log in, ask the system to create something new, check if something exists, change something, or delete something, and then log out.

sections.title: Protocol Structure
sections.content:
EPP messages are written in XML, an easy-to-parse text format. A server greets a client with a greeting message that advertises the services, object types, and extensions it supports. The greeting also includes the server's data collection policies.

A client authenticates with a login command, specifying a client identifier, password, and protocol version. After successful login, the client can send commands (such as create, delete, check, info, update, renew, and transfer). The server responds to each command with a response containing a result code (a four-digit number), a human-readable message, and optional response data. The client logs out with a logout command.
sections.eli5: EPP conversations follow a pattern: the server says hello and what it can do, the client says who it is, the client gives orders, the server answers, and finally the client says goodbye.

sections.title: Commands and Operations
sections.content:
EPP defines two categories of commands: session management commands (login and logout) and object management commands. Object management commands fall into two types: query commands (read-only) and transform commands (write operations).

Query commands are check (determine if an object can be created), info (retrieve details about an object), poll (receive queued messages from the server), and transfer (query a transfer status). Transform commands are create (instantiate a new object), delete (remove an object), renew (extend an object's validity period), update (modify an object's attributes), and transfer (change object sponsorship). Transform commands may be processed offline, in which case the server returns a response code of 1001 (action pending) and later sends a service message when the action completes.
sections.eli5: EPP has two kinds of orders. Read orders ask questions: does this thing exist, what does it look like, what messages do I have, is this transfer still waiting? Write orders make changes: create this new thing, delete that thing, make this thing last longer, change something about this thing, or give this thing to someone else.

sections.title: Extensibility and Object Mappings
sections.content:
EPP's power lies in its extensibility. The base protocol defines the structure and semantics of commands and responses, but object-specific details are pushed into separate object mappings. For example, the create command in the base protocol is generic, but domain-specific create parameters are defined in an EPP domain name mapping (such as RFC 3731). This design allows EPP to support any object type—domain names, hosts, contacts, or custom objects—without modifying the base protocol.

An EPP server announces which object types it supports in its greeting, using XML namespaces and schema URIs. Clients request which objects they wish to work with during login. Extensions can be added at the protocol level (server-defined features), at the object level (custom behavior for an object type), or at the command-response level (custom data in a command or response).
sections.eli5: EPP is like a template system. The base protocol is the template for asking and answering, but the details of what you're managing are described in separate instruction sheets. You can plug in any type of thing to manage without changing the core system.

sections.title: Result Codes and Response Handling
sections.content:
Every EPP response includes a result code (a four-digit decimal number) and a human-readable message. The first digit indicates success (1xxx) or failure (2xxx). The second digit groups the response into a category: protocol syntax (x0zz), implementation rules (x1zz), security (x2zz), data management (x3zz), server system (x4zz), or connection management (x5zz). The third and fourth digits provide specific detail.

Common success codes are 1000 (command completed successfully), 1001 (action pending), 1300 (no messages in queue), and 1500 (session ending). Common error codes include 2001 (command syntax error), 2002 (command use error), 2200 (authentication error), 2302 (object already exists), 2303 (object does not exist), and 2304 (object status prohibits operation).
sections.eli5: Every answer from the server comes with a code number that tells you whether your order worked. Codes starting with 1 mean success, codes starting with 2 mean something went wrong. The other numbers give you more specific details.

sections.title: Security and Design Properties
sections.content:
EPP is designed for use over secure, reliable transports such as TLS-protected TCP. The protocol does not define transport or security mechanisms; those are specified separately. Clients and servers authenticate using plain-text passwords delivered out-of-band before first login.

A key design property is idempotency: each transform command is designed so that executing it multiple times produces the same final state as executing it once. This allows clients to safely retry commands when a response is lost or delayed. Another design property is that EPP commands are atomic: they either fully succeed or fully fail, never leaving an object in a partially updated state. The protocol also supports pending operations, allowing servers to defer action completion (for example, to await human approval) while immediately acknowledging receipt of the command.
sections.eli5: EPP is meant to run over an encrypted connection. Orders are all-or-nothing: if something goes wrong partway through, the whole order is undone. If you accidentally send the same order twice, it has the same effect as sending it once.
